notYet: Not yet part of the Eastern Mediterranean

stages.name: Villages & herders
stages.desc: Farming villages and pastoral peoples outside the palace system

stages.name: Palace kingdom
stages.desc: Kings, palaces, scribes and royal long-distance trade

stages.name: Egyptian control
stages.desc: Egypt and the lands it ruled or garrisoned

stages.name: Destroyed or abandoned
stages.desc: Palaces burned or deserted; towns shrink or vanish

stages.name: Sea Peoples settlement
stages.desc: Philistines and other newcomers from the Aegean world

stages.name: Phoenician city-state
stages.desc: Independent coastal cities living by trade

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Alashiya: copper-exporting towns at Enkomi, Kition and Hala Sultan Tekke
Coastal towns are attacked; several are destroyed or abandoned
Rebuilt towns such as Kition show Aegean-style pottery and newcomers from the Aegean

states.name: Israel
timeline: Canaanite city-states under Egyptian garrisons at Beth Shean and Megiddo
Hazor, the largest Canaanite city, is burned
Philistines settle Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron; Egypt keeps inland garrisons for a time
Megiddo and Lachish are destroyed as Egyptian rule ends

states.name: Palestine
timeline: Gaza is Egypt's headquarters in Canaan; few villages in the hills
Merneptah's stele names a people called Israel in Canaan
Egypt withdraws; new villages spread through the highlands, while Gaza becomes a Philistine city

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Byblos, Sidon and Tyre are vassal cities of Egypt
Egypt's hold slips; the coastal cities come through the crisis on their own
Byblos and Sidon pay tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I
Byblos refuses to give Egypt cedar without payment

states.name: Syria
timeline: Ugarit and Carchemish, vassal kingdoms of the Hittites; Arwad on its island
Ugarit is destroyed and never reoccupied
Emar on the Euphrates is burned
Inland, Aramaean groups spread; on the coast, island Arwad survives and pays tribute to Assyria

states.name: Turkey
timeline: The Hittite Great Kingdom rules Anatolia from Hattusa
Hattusa is abandoned and burned; the Hittite empire is gone
Only small successor kingdoms such as Carchemish and Melid survive in the south-east

states.name: Greece
timeline: Mycenaean palaces at Mycenae, Pylos, Thebes and Tiryns rule through scribes and storerooms
Palaces burn across mainland Greece; Pylos falls about 1180
Population falls sharply; Linear B writing is forgotten for four centuries

states.name: Jordan
timeline: Villages and herders east of the Jordan
Copper smelting grows at Faynan as Cypriot supplies falter

states.name: Egypt
timeline: Ramesses II rules Egypt and much of Canaan
Merneptah defeats Libyans and northern sea raiders
Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples at the Delta
Ramesses III is murdered in a harem plot
The New Kingdom ends; Egypt divides between Tanis and Thebes

events.title: Lion Gate
events.text: Mycenae's walls are extended and its Lion Gate built, around 1250 BC.

events.title: Ramesses II rules
events.text: Ramesses II rules from his Delta capital, at peace with the Hittites since their treaty of 1259 BC.

events.title: Hattusa
events.text: The Hittite capital holds great temples, tablet archives and underground granaries.

events.title: Letters of Ugarit
events.text: Ugarit's archives hold letters in Akkadian and in the city's own cuneiform alphabet.

events.title: Hazor burns
events.text: Hazor, the largest city in Canaan, is destroyed by fire; who burned it is debated.

events.title: Trade embargo
events.text: The Hittite king forbids Amurru to let Assyrian merchants or Ahhiyawan ships pass.

events.title: Grain for Hatti
events.text: Pharaoh Merneptah ships grain to keep the Hittite kingdom alive through famine.

events.title: Merneptah's victory
events.text: Merneptah defeats Libyans allied with northern peoples: Sherden, Shekelesh, Ekwesh, Lukka and Teresh.

events.title: Israel named
events.text: Merneptah's victory stele names Israel for the first time.

events.title: Gelidonya wreck
events.text: A small ship carrying copper ingots and scrap bronze sinks off southern Anatolia.

events.title: Sea battle
events.text: The last Hittite king, Suppiluliuma II, fights enemy ships off Alashiya, Cyprus.

events.title: Three dry years
events.text: Tree rings from Gordion record exceptional drought from about 1198 to 1196 BC.

events.title: A matter of life
events.text: The Hittite king demands grain shipped to the port of Ura: a matter of life and death.

events.title: Seven enemy ships
events.text: Ugarit's king writes to Alashiya that seven enemy ships have ravaged his land.

events.title: Ugarit destroyed
events.text: Ugarit is burned and abandoned, never to be rebuilt.

events.title: Gibala falls
events.text: Ugarit's southern port is destroyed; its pollen layers record the long drought.

events.title: Mycenae burns
events.text: Fire, and perhaps earthquake, ruins the citadel of Mycenae.

events.title: Tiryns endures
events.text: Tiryns's palace burns, but its lower town is rebuilt and grows.

events.title: Hattusa abandoned
events.text: The Hittite court leaves its capital, which is later burned.

events.title: Emar burns
events.text: Emar on the Euphrates is destroyed; tablets in the ruins date its last years.

events.title: Enkomi attacked
events.text: Enkomi and other Cypriot towns are attacked and partly destroyed.

events.title: Pylos burns
events.text: Fire destroys the palace of Pylos, baking its clay Linear B tablets hard.

events.title: Troy falls
events.text: The city of Troy VIIa is destroyed by fire.

events.title: Carchemish survives
events.text: Kuzi-Teshub, of the Hittite royal line, keeps Carchemish as a kingdom.

events.title: Battle of the Delta
events.text: In his eighth year, Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples by land and at the Nile mouths.

events.title: Medinet Habu
events.text: Ramesses III's temple at Thebes carves the battle and names the invaders.

events.title: Philistines at Ashdod
events.text: Newcomers with Aegean-style pottery, hearths and pork settle Ashdod and Ekron.

events.title: Ashkelon's newcomers
events.text: Ancient DNA shows Ashkelon's early Iron Age people carried new, southern European ancestry.

events.title: Timna mines
events.text: Egyptian expeditions still mine copper at Timna under Ramesses III.

events.title: Workers' strike
events.text: Tomb builders at Deir el-Medina down tools when their grain rations fail.

events.title: Ramesses III murdered
events.text: The pharaoh is killed in a plot hatched in his own harem.

events.title: Kassite Babylon falls
events.text: Elamite invaders end the Kassite dynasty of Babylon.

events.title: Kition rebuilt
events.text: Kition on Cyprus is rebuilt, with new temples and Aegean-style wares.

events.title: Purple at Sarepta
events.text: Workshops at Sarepta crush murex shells for the purple dye of Phoenicia.

events.title: Egypt leaves Canaan
events.text: The last Egyptian garrisons, such as Beth Shean, are given up.

events.title: Megiddo destroyed
events.text: Megiddo's Canaanite city is destroyed, and Lachish soon after.

events.title: Faynan copper
events.text: Copper smelting grows in the Faynan valley, a new source as old routes fail.

events.title: Assyria at the sea
events.text: Tiglath-Pileser I sails in Arwad's ships and takes tribute from Arwad, Byblos and Sidon.

events.title: Tjeker at Dor
events.text: Dor on the Carmel coast is a harbour of the Tjeker, one of the Sea Peoples.

events.title: Wenamun at Byblos
events.text: Byblos's king makes Egypt's envoy pay for cedar; Sidon has fifty ships at sea.

events.title: New Kingdom ends
events.text: After Ramesses XI, Egypt is split between kings at Tanis and priests at Thebes.

events.title: Tyre rising
events.text: Tyre, on its island, emerges as a leading Phoenician trading city.

chartNote: Share of the area of nine present-day countries, by the fate of each one's main Bronze Age centres. Regions are today's boundaries: a simplification, since within one country some towns burned while others survived (island Arwad lies in today's Syria, Gaza in Palestine). Egypt's large area weighs heavily, and destruction dates are approximate.
